summary:
Ebonyi State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch records that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The Act also criminalises attending, organising or promoting same-sex weddings and registering or publicly promoting gay groups.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Ebonyi is not among the states that have adopted Sharia, so the death-penalty provisions do not apply there; the federal maximum of 14 years is the operative exposure for a visitor in Ebonyi.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Enforcement against LGBTQ+ people is documented nationally. Human Rights Watch found that the SSMPA's passage on 7 January 2014 was immediately followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detention across the country, including the arrest without charge of 21 young men at a birthday gathering in Ibadan and repeated police detentions reported elsewhere. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

If detained, placement between male and female sections is left to discretion. Press coverage of Bobrisky's (Idris Okuneye) imprisonment in 2024 openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in; she was held in a maximum-security prison in Lagos.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice, as reported by Sahara Reporters (19 August 2026), warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
Criminalisation predates independence: same-sex sexual activity has been illegal since 1904 in the Northern Region and since 1916 region-wide, and the SSMPA reinforced that colonial-era base rather than creating it.

The same UK advisory warns that mobile networks can be suspended and curfews imposed with little notice. That measure is not directed at LGBT+ people, but it removes the communication channels on which a visitor relying on apps or a check-in contact would depend.

Ebonyi's position differs from the northern states in degree, not in kind. The federal term of up to 14 years applies in both; only the religious criminal law states add the death penalty. Ebonyi-specific enforcement is absent from these sources while other states carry documented cases, so the absence of reported incidents in Ebonyi should not be read as evidence of tolerance.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ebonyi live under the same statutes as visitors, with no state-level protection against discrimination, hate-motivated violence or dismissal on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Human Rights Watch records that after the SSMPA came into force, LGBT Nigerians faced mob attacks, arbitrary arrest, extortion and police detention in their homes and social venues, and that those interviewed described repeated detentions.

Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Community organising carries direct criminal exposure: operating, participating in or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations is punishable by 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and registering or publicly promoting a gay group is itself an offence under the SSMPA.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Ebonyi-specific statute, enforcement action, court decision or protection measure is identified in the sources reviewed. Whether the SSMPA has been charged or prosecuted in Ebonyi State is unresolved and not sourced here.

Whether the 2022 proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have been enacted into law is unresolved; the sources available record the proposals and the fear they produced, not their legislative outcome.

Reports of threats and raids alongside informal community organising among Nigerian queer people appear in the record as a fetch-time summary of a national feature, and no primary text was available to verify whether any of those incidents occurred in Ebonyi State.

The sources do not establish how Ebonyi State's police or correctional authorities handle placement of a trans detainant between male and female sections; the only placement evidence in the record concerns a prison in Lagos.
